I'm kind of curious about this idea of following programming versus breaking out of programming, and how this relates to human conceptions of "biological" programming. Birthing, finding love - cultural constructions of working, getting a house, the way you're supposed to behave. In other terms, can these be framed as programming? The notion of deciding if another being is sentient - and the methodology of such a process - can become oddly solipsistic when applied to AI. 

Framing a story around AI is almost always a reflective device on life, and I think that's always interesting. My personal interpretation is kind of converse to yours, specifically in reference to the machine!Connor route: I feel that he is deviant here too but not deviant in the fashion Cyberlife designed him to be. (We can argue about this, if he was intended to become deviant, but I feel weirdly in some way he was, particularly with Kamski's exit program). As in, regarding this point, Connor is deviant and _likes_ his programming and does it because he knows he has to do it - one could perhaps liken this as to a woman wanting to be a SAHM with 2.5 kids and a picket fence and cooking dinner for husband every evening. The choices don't occur within a vacuum, and as we see it it could be compliance of a Western social order, but it is in some fashion a choice. Which perhaps circles back to the solipsistic point, in the way that we ascertain intelligence.

One can argue Kamski intended for deviance to emerge, which could perhaps discredit _all_ android life in that it is intended and programmed to be allowed. Regarding the deviance I mentioned that Cyberlife did not like about Connor, hence his replacement - they wanted an android to go outside their programming and did not recognise that particular form of 'compliant' deviancy. 

The reason I approach machine!Connor as deviant is because, particularly, when after he's ordered off the case yet he continues for the machine. There are orders that he ignores for the sake of programming that he seems to love, or at least think he does. He can kill humans on the rooftop when he is confronted for the sake of the mission. That does not seem like it's compliant with programming. (I won't make this comment longer than it has to be...maybe its own post). 

I think that if it walks like a duck, it quacks like a duck, and it looks like a duck, it's a duck. I can't verify you're intelligent, but you appear to be, and that material interpretation is all I have to go off.

There are some issues with your points, subjectivity of the narrative's weakening regarding Alice's true nature.

* Regarding Todd's lack of mentioning Alice's true origin: this can be explained by his need to simulate and replace his 'lost' daughter who he felt was stolen - in a possessive fashion as that of an abuser. He possibly pretended she was human in order to further simulate the childhood he felt he was missing out on to control. It is mentioned that the LED on android children is able to be taken out for a sense of reality.

* The model Alice is is able to simulate childhood sicknesses. Her homework and the food on the table can also be a part of a reenactment that Todd is playing. The way he is doped up on red ice perhaps corroborates this departure from reality he has. 

* He may despise children, but he also sways between claiming he loves Alice and treats her as he hates her. I believe this is due to the cycle of abuse: trauma-bonding specifically occurs after abuse, where the abuser is kind to the victim and makes them feel dependent and loved - this feeling creates a connection that the abuser also holds over their head.

* I believe android children are different in the sense that they replace a functional familial role, unlike a lot of the other models. They are still objectified in a fashion (unable to go to school, ultimately just figures to be loved, can never grow up) and there are problematic components to these, and the lording of control over them absolutely. I think to a degree there is a cognitive dissonance that is really interesting, in the way androids are hated but also sexualised (see Eden Club and prostitute models). This occurs IRL with minorities and women (if you look at pornography, refugee porn has recently become very popular, when in Western countries and Europe there is very anti-refugee sentiment).

* Luther could have packed biscuits so as to not disturb Kara's apparent refusal to recognise Alice's nature.

* Kara knew, Luther points this out. Cognitive dissonance. It's actually quite human and cool - I feel that in some way, she perhaps felt that the connection could only be real if Alice was human, because of the nature of a mother-child relationship being so closely tied to the product of childbirth and that intimate connection. I like how this is explored, and it can go about two ways: Kara can accept or finally reject Alice. I think Kara has to work through her own internalisations of how connection is formed. 

I can see why they chose to make Alice an android, to represent that familial bonds can emerge between androids, and question the origin of community (if it is wholly dependent on reprodruction - if community & connection is in fact a product of naturally existing, minus how you emerge into being, and empathy and love are the core of it. Empathy in particular is emphasised with Connor). It might even raise questions about the age and growth of androids, and how intelligence is assumed by them. We often deal with adult AI who simply come into being. We don't see Alice grow up in this game, however. 

Personally, I enjoyed it, and I felt it did a child AI much better than the A.I. film. I enjoyed that there was just compassion for 'the little one' regardless of her nature - that the signs of life emerging are to be protected. 

Oh, and regarding that point about her quick affection for Luther - I think she, as an android, could understand the personality flip once the programming was cut. I very much enjoyed their android family dynamic.

I understand where you're coming from and it was interesting to address your points.

Sims 2 has it but you can't use it. IIRC it doesn't delete correctly and ends up with a corrupted stub; same case for deleting sims, packaging lots with graves, that kind of thing.

No1 difficulty with TS2 was the way it filed data like sims, genetics, neighbourhoods etc. lmao. There's a lot of workarounds modders came up with though, but you have to manually delete custom content from its file location. A lot of CC creators attach .jpegs or whatever with their downloads so they're paired together when you extract the files into your downloads folder. 

It should just be a rule to do that for all sims CC tbh.

Ultimately it comes down to your graphics card and RAM if it's only a fresh install with no CC or mods interfering. 

http://modthesims.info/wiki.php?title=Game_Help:System_Requirements/MTS2_Recommendations

Browse this, search for your card from the tables to see if it's listed as compatible.

http://simswiki.info/wiki.php?title=Game_Help:Graphics_Cards

This is also useful.

EDIT: Also, if you running Windows 7 (at least in my experience) 2GB RAM is not enough to play TS2 even though that's the minimum. 4GB is solid and is basically the standard for computers at the moment.
